topic: Family Law: Uniform Civil Code (UCC) and Special Marriage Act, 1954
description: This module covers the secular frameworks of family law in India. It examines the constitutional mandate for a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) aimed at harmonizing personal laws, and details the Special Marriage Act, 1954, which allows individuals of different faiths to marry without religious conversion.

key_points: Constitutional Mandate: Article 44 of the Indian Constitution, under the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), states that 'The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.'

Objective: A UCC aims to replace the fragmented, religion-based personal laws (Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption) with a single, common set of secular laws applicable to all citizens equally.

Non-Justiciable Nature: Being a DPSP (Part IV of the Constitution), Article 44 is non-justiciable, meaning it cannot be legally enforced by any court, though it is fundamental in the governance of the country.

Current Status: While India does not have a national UCC, the State of Goa retains a common family law (Goa Civil Code) inherited from the Portuguese. Recently, states like Uttarakhand have enacted their own state-level UCCs.

special_marriage_act_nature.concept: The Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA): Nature and Applicability
key_points: Secular Legislation: The SMA provides a special form of marriage that is purely secular and statutory. It is the primary law used for inter-faith and inter-caste marriages.

No Religious Conversion Required: Unlike religious personal laws, the SMA allows two individuals of different religions (e.g., a Hindu and a Muslim) to marry each other while retaining their respective religious identities. No religious ceremonies or conversions are legally required.

Conditions for Marriage: Similar to other marriage laws, neither party must have a living spouse, both must be capable of giving valid consent, the male must be 21 and female 18, and they must not be within degrees of prohibited relationship.

The 30-Day Notice Period: Parties intending to marry under the SMA must give written notice to the Marriage Officer of the district where at least one party has resided for 30 days. This notice is published, inviting public objections for a period of 30 days.
Grounds for Objection: Anyone can object to the marriage, but only on the legal grounds that it violates the essential conditions (e.g., underage, existing spouse).

Impact on Succession: A major legal consequence of an inter-faith marriage under the SMA is that the property succession of the couple (and their future children) is no longer governed by their respective religious personal laws, but by the secular Indian Succession Act, 1925.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution directs the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) for the citizens throughout the territory of India?
questions.explanation: Article 44 is placed in Part IV of the Constitution (Directive Principles of State Policy) and explicitly directs the State to endeavor to secure a Uniform Civil Code.

questions.question: Rahul (a Hindu) and Zara (a Muslim) wish to marry under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 without changing their religions. After they submit their notice of intended marriage to the Marriage Officer, how long is the mandatory waiting period before the marriage can be legally solemnized?
questions.explanation: Under the Special Marriage Act, a mandatory 30-day notice period is required after the publication of the notice of intended marriage. This allows time for any valid legal objections to be raised before the marriage is solemnized.

questions.question: If a Hindu man and a Christian woman marry under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, which law will govern the inheritance and succession of their property after their death?

options.C: The property goes to the State.
options.D: The personal law of the husband automatically applies to both.

questions.explanation: A critical consequence of inter-faith marriages under the Special Marriage Act is that the parties are severed from their religious personal succession laws. Their property inheritance is strictly governed by the secular Indian Succession Act, 1925.
